entry_finding: Catalog line 27. The strophe repeats its music while its words change. Those features coexist in each verse; they are not two successive spans. Introductory or closing material need not change that principle.
Catalog line 28. The changing text and the stable ending occur inside the same verse. The source permits a final line or couplet. This diagram describes a tail refrain; other placements also occur.
Catalog line 29. A recurring strophe supplies the norm against which one verse changes melody or key. The altered verse is often last but has no prescribed place here.
Catalog line 30. Verses advance the story. ABCB and AABB are common quatrain schemes in this entry; refrain and terminal twist are possible, with no fixed number of verses.
Catalog line 31. Four equal eight-bar sections yield the named 32-bar return. Title placement describes A’s text, not a distinct section; title lyric is typical rather than a universal AABA test.
Catalog line 32. The AABA cycle gains another bridge and final A. The second B may be a solo, and a title tag may follow. Extension does not establish the bar length of every instance.
Catalog line 33. The source specifies 32 bars overall, with B continuing the first A, the return of A, and the title at the new C ending. It gives no bar count for each part.

Catalog line 34. An introductory verse may be cut in performance. The main refrain can be 16 or 32 bars; AABA and ABAC are alternative common shapes. The source does not pair just one length with one shape.

Catalog line 35. AAB organizes the words of this lyric example across a 12-bar cycle. The repeat may change slightly and the answer rhymes. Twelve bars alone do not entail words or a particular rhyme; solos can intervene between stanzas.

Catalog line 36. Two alternatives are explicit: statement and answer, or a couplet with short refrain. The separate two-lines field does not resolve whether that refrain occupies an additional lyric line. No count is assigned to that alternative.

Catalog line 37. AAAB is a specific quatrain scheme, whereas “a quatrain” states only the line count. The unschemed four-line option is left open. A stop-time verse before a 12-bar refrain is an optional larger arrangement, not a mandatory subdivision.
Catalog line 38. The verse and recurring title chorus alternate over shared harmony. Words such as “same chords” describe the relation across sections rather than a third section.
Catalog line 39. The chorus differs melodically and harmonically. The catalog’s higher, fuller chorus is a characteristic sound, not an additional nested unit.
Catalog line 40. The prechorus builds from verse toward chorus within the cycle. The 2–4-line figure belongs to this catalog example; prechorus function alone does not prescribe a line count.

Catalog line 41. The full prose maps to ABABCB if A is verse, B chorus and C bridge. The listed ABCABCDC alias lacks a letter key and does not follow that mapping. Only the described example is encoded.

Catalog line 42. The catalog models a cycle with prechorus and post-chorus, then bridge and chorus. A post-chorus follows a chorus; its presence alone does not require all the other sections in that example.
Catalog line 43. The chorus is heard before the first verse and a verse–chorus cycle follows. An opening hook qualifies only if that passage is the chorus; an isolated hook is insufficient.
Catalog line 44. The form can replace a bridge with an instrumental solo or place the solo beside a bridge. “Beside” specifies no before/after order.

Catalog line 45. The catalog repeats the A–B pair. Two reprises are also commonly repeated separately, yielding AABB. The agreed part of both accounts is the division into two main sections; repeat order must be specified independently.
Catalog line 46. A contrasting middle lies between the first A and its return. The final A may be shortened.
Catalog line 47. The two matching Stollen form the opening pair within each stanza. The closing Abgesang contrasts and is longer in this source.
Catalog line 48. The returning A separates episodes. ABACA and ABACABA are explicitly offered as alternative examples, so C or a fixed number of episodes is not a required ending condition.
Catalog line 49. The outward sections, central climax and reversed return are correctly nested for the listed ABCBA example. The row describes mirror ordering, not a required five-section count.
Catalog line 50. The diagram is one four-section example. The constraint applies to the recurrence of entire sections, not to all rhythmic or motivic resemblances.
Catalog line 51. Several internally formed sub-songs share one track with joins between them; a return of the opening theme is optional and the number of sub-songs is unspecified.
Catalog line 52. Several whole songs or excerpts occur in succession. The diagram uses two illustrative items; no two-song ceiling, fixed excerpt length or universal joining device follows.

Catalog line 53. The two independent tunes can sound together. The catalog introduces each separately first, then combines them; separate full statements are a feature of this example. The two simultaneous voices share the final span.

Catalog line 54. The source describes new words fitted to existing music. Stanza shape, rhyme points and stresses are concurrent text-fitting constraints for the catalog example, not a sequence of sung sections.
Catalog line 55. The item list is the substance of the verses, tied by a recurrent title or refrain. Neither line placement nor the number of items is fixed.

Catalog line 56. Rapid, densely rhymed delivery is the described technique. The slower returning refrain and possible acceleration belong to the supplied example; this source alone cannot establish either as essential to all patter songs.

Catalog line 57. The row supplies an eight-line verse and fixed singalong chorus, with optional patter between. This is a catalog scenario for music-hall repertoire; no evidence in the row makes that length compulsory across the genre.
Catalog line 58. The title refrain ends each eight-line verse in the catalog’s two- or three-verse scenario. This is an example of the genre; the row does not specify identical music in every verse.

Catalog line 59. The stage-number scenario orders introductory verse, 32-bar refrain, dance break and returned refrain capped by a button. A key rise is optional. The catalog gives one arrangement, not an exhaustive grammar of dance numbers.
Catalog line 60. Song, sung dialogue and underscored speech intertwine with action. The rule groups materials without assigning an unsupported order to the scene or the return of a theme.

Catalog line 61. The row orders the first two verse roles, gives the chorus to both singers and assigns trading to the bridge. It does not fix the location of every chorus or bridge. The role view avoids enforcing the literal display order.
Catalog line 62. Speech-like delivery in irregular sung lines is the defining material here. Separation of set songs is a common context in the row rather than a full-work sequence.
Catalog line 63. The passage lies between recitative and aria in delivery. These are qualities of one passage, not first and second sections of arioso.
Catalog line 64. The first A and B use the two text parts; A is then performed again with ornamentation. Text divisions and performed sections must not be counted as if they were the same object.
Catalog line 65. The speech overlaps a continuous musical accompaniment and may turn into song. The rule view does not imply that the accompaniment stops during speech.
Catalog line 66. Spoken scenes are interrupted by airs using new words to familiar melodies. The text/music relation is inside an air, not a sequence of two sounding sections.

Catalog line 67. Songs and spoken verse are performance media rather than a compulsory opening section. The example distinguishes an antimasque, main masque, revels and closing song. Section order and media are shown separately; this does not prescribe one sequence for every masque.
Catalog line 68. A sequence of separate songs has its own ordering under a common theme or narrative. Internal form belongs to each song, with no fixed movement count here.
Catalog line 69. Recitative, aria, duet and chorus are movement types available in the catalog’s cantata. They do not have to occur in the printed order. A closing chorus is described as usual.
Catalog line 70. The sacred narrative is divided into parts containing vocal forms. The row specifies an unstaged dramatic setting but no order or number for recitatives, arias or choruses.
Catalog line 71. The catalog example follows head–solos–head. A head arrangement instead identifies how players work out an arrangement and retain it in memory. Either may occur without the other.

Catalog line 72. Words are fitted to the note sequence of a recorded instrumental improvisation. A preceding head is part of one possible realization. The word-to-note mapping imposes no such whole-song ordering.
Catalog line 73. The short held-note ending is the catalog’s 2–4-line tag example. This source does not demonstrate that every barbershop tag has that line count.

Catalog line 74. The row gives an eight-bar hook and a typically sixteen-bar rap verse, with eight-, twelve- and twenty-four-bar verse alternatives and optional framing. The lengths characterize this example, not all rap.
Catalog line 75. One or more long verses proceed without a hook. Beat switches are optional; the catalog’s “often 32 bars or more” does not create a lower bound.

Catalog line 76. The defining organization distributes verses successively to different rappers. A shared hook may be present, but the row gives no location for it. An unordered rule avoids making the hook a closing event.

Catalog line 77. Two rappers alternate. Three rounds each is customary in this row, not compulsory. Set-ups and punchlines can recur within a verse; only the climactic final line has an assigned position here.

Catalog line 78. Freestyle describes improvisation here; cypher adds turn-taking among performers. The catalog describes an underlying loop but provides no fixed sections. It does not show that all freestyle is a group exchange.
Catalog line 79. Chants, shout-outs and a returning hook occur over the riddim. The row establishes no fixed verse size or hook location, so a rule view is appropriate.

Catalog line 80. The specified intro, two build/drop cycles and outro give one dance arrangement. A verse and a breakdown are alternatives within the first cycle. No evidence in the row requires this count or these bar lengths across EDM.
Catalog line 81. The riff supplies the repeating ground, with chants and occasional refrain. A break interrupts the groove; its position and duration are deliberately unspecified.

Catalog line 82. The source orders verse and chorus before an extended vamp and closing tag. It allows a bridge somewhere before the vamp without locking its position. Lead improvisation and repeated choir material occur simultaneously.

Catalog line 83. Topical or storytelling verses and a fixed chorus form the row’s calypso example. Its usual eight-line verse count is descriptive. The entry gives no basis for a universal genre-wide pattern.
Catalog line 84. A contest with two singers trading improvised topical calypso stanzas is an example. The source distinguishes contest exchange from the broader fact of improvisation.
Catalog line 85. The source’s short advertising example proceeds from set-up to hook to a sung brand tag. The 15–60-second field is the given example range, not a test for every jingle.
Catalog line 86. A short text repeats; the catalog usually borrows an existing tune and sometimes supplies a caller. The leader is an optional performer, not an extra line at the end of the chant.
Catalog line 87. Couplets, spelling and exchange describe the cheer’s materials, with a shout at the end. No interior order or compulsory count is stated.

ABCB is the rhyme scheme of successive lines in the catalog’s ballad stanza, not four constituent sections. Narrative singing is the broader genre; individual ballads and versions need not use this quatrain.

Four four-stress lines fit long metre when iambic. The catalog also lists paired fourteen-syllable lines. Split 8 + 6, these give common-measure rhythm; the diagram omits that conflicting alternative.
A fixed refrain line recurs inside each stanza, interleaved with changing narrative or dialogue lines.
Variants preserve a recurring verbal frame while changing phrases. A question-and-answer exchange can culminate in a final revelation; exact wording and ending vary.

The printed sheet is the means of circulation. The catalog sketches an address, topical narrative and moral on a known air; the Library of Congress documents that singers could supply or change the tune.
The initial address opens the narrative. A moral and a farewell are alternative endings, with no fixed stanza count supplied.
First person is the narrator’s voice. The catalog places the warning within a confession and specifies a final farewell stanza.
Stanzas carry fragments of a narrative and return to a final refrain line. The account of a real event describes the subject, not a separate section.
The couplet or quatrain is half-spoken over the figure; the punchline closes that unit rather than adding a compulsory extra line.
The AABB story stanza has an optional following couplet. Scots work setting and comic subject describe the text, not additional sections.

Leisure singing aboard ship distinguishes the forebitter from a shanty used to coordinate work. A chorus is possible; the row leaves the size and ordering of its verses open. Section B names five shanties; this sixth maritime entry is explicitly a leisure song.
The sung verses interrupt the spoken narrative at significant moments. The row does not prescribe how many interruptions there are.
The introductions, combat, revival and collection trace the hero-combat example. Other mumming plays have different action and roles.
The introductions name a dancer per stanza. A final call for the dance or for money is a choice of endings.

The visit’s greeting, explanation and petition are text functions. The chorus is common, but its placement and frequency are unspecified. An unplaced chorus cannot be drawn after the petition as a required endpoint.
The repeated unit is one sales phrase occupying one or two lines; an additional answer or verse is unspecified.
The row specifies short mourning stanzas and a returning cry. It gives no fixed placement for the burden within or between stanzas.
A leader’s line cues a group reply. In liturgical use this is responsorial; alternating choir groups exemplify antiphonal singing.
A leader and crew alternate while hauling. The cited performance account describes two exchanges. The catalog’s separate inter-verse chorus and its frequency remain unverified for this pattern.
This short-haul example gives the solo line one brief group response. The stressed pull word is inside that response.
The catalog pairs solo and crew lines inside a verse, with a larger chorus after the verse. Its use at a capstan identifies its function.
The row describes continuous alternating voices while the crew walks. It stipulates no verse boundary for this example.
The response follows a solo couplet inside the longer pattern the catalog describes. Pumping is the work being done; an exact couplet length is an example.
The lead line and fixed answer form the exchange timed to the stroke. AAB is described as frequent, not prescribed for every performance.
The catalog illustrates a solo call, pause and another phrase in free rhythm. Archival accounts also document replies between workers in separate fields.
The lead line and group answer on vocables repeat as a cycle. No count of cycles is specified.
The marching group echoes or answers the leader. Footsteps govern timing rather than adding a third musical section.
An echo is a verbatim group return of the leader’s words. No fixed verse length follows from that rule.
An invariant frame and a substitution slot coexist within one verse. Only the word in that slot changes between iterations.
The catalog illustrates newest-first recapitulation after adding each item. The entry supplies a progression, not an initial list length.
The row explicitly calls this example cumulative. It accumulates numbered items, counts back to one and specifies a fixed closing tag.
A number goes down once per repeat of the same verse. Descending numbers alone do not imply accumulation of prior verses.
The answer stanzas follow the group of riddle stanzas in the same order in the described arrangement.
The vocables belong to the refrain; the row does not give a line count or specify its exact position.
The catalog describes soothing quatrains and a framing refrain. That pattern illustrates one shape within a genre defined by function.

AABB and ABCB are examples for the common quatrain. The row permits two to eight lines, so neither four lines nor either scheme is universal. The displayed example selects AABB; ABCB is an alternative, not an extra fifth leaf.
The chant allocates one beat per child and ends on an elimination word. The word belongs to the chant’s ending.
The strict rhythm applies to either couplets or quatrains. The counting or spelling tail is a separate closing unit. The choice of initial unit occupies one position.
Each verse names an action, followed by a returning chorus between verses. The action is the verse content.
Lines are paired with gestures. Body-part substitutions in later verses describe variation across repeats, not an extra section.
The chant accelerates toward a closing drop line. The source gives a range of four to eight lines.
The whole one- or two-line taunt repeats. No reply or fixed repeat count is given.
Similar sounds crowd a one- to four-line text. Beyond that constraint the order of words and sections is open.
Players trade ritual insults. Rhymed line pairs occur in the catalog’s verse example. Recorded practice also uses unrhymed speech.
A set opening leads to the recited narrative and a closing boast. Four-beat rhymed couplets are the narrative building blocks.
A conventional seven-part singing call puts the middle break between two pairs of figures, rather than after all four. Around 64 beats per part is customary.
The caller fits instructions to the beat. Traditional patter can use rhyming couplets and extra words; rhyme is a technique rather than a requirement for every call.
Delayed entries of a common melody overlap and can loop. A round is a looping kind of canon; the voices are concurrent once they enter.
The pun comes from words sounding together after staggered entries. The source identifies the catch as a comic round.
A following voice imitates a leading voice after a delay. The imitation can be strict or free. A canon can end or repeat cyclically.
The catalog describes a short polyphonic lyric treated continuously with a repeated final line. “Part-song” here names a texture, not a Victorian form.
The half-stanza including its fa-la ending repeats; the repetition encloses both text and refrain. “Part-song” does not imply Victorian authorship or form.
Two or three voices and recurring stanzas with repeated sections characterize the catalog example. Voice count is a scoring detail, not a sequence.
The recurring stanza shape belongs to a solo voice with lute. ABABCC is optional in the row.
The strophic solo is accompanied by viols. The whole group enters for a repeat of the last lines in this account.
Three voices sing successive stanzas with a refrain. Its position within the stanza is unspecified.
An unaccompanied ensemble sings contrasting, through-composed sections. The number and order of contrasts are unspecified.
This entry explicitly identifies a Victorian setting with strophic chordal choir texture. The wider term part-song does not by itself establish a link to this subtype.
The stage jig uses ballad stanzas across several tunes. Changing tunes, characters and dancing are staging features rather than successive text units.
An opening two- to four-line burden precedes the first stanza and returns after each stanza. AAAB and AABB are alternative stanza rhymes.
A returning cradle-song burden characterizes this entry. Dialogue is possible; its placement relative to the opening is unspecified.
Christmas is the occasion. The row offers hymn-like stanzas with either a short refrain or a chorus; it does not locate either within the stanza.
The languages alternate within an otherwise independently chosen song design. A refrain is a possible switch point, not a required container.
Stanzas share a tune and a metrical profile. The linked metres are alternatives. Some settings close with a doxology.
A metrical stanza and the recurring refrain are successive units. The row does not give a specific hymn metre.
The catalog illustrates four lines of verse followed by a four-line title chorus. This is one arrangement within the broader gospel repertoire.
Some settings add a refrain to inherited hymn stanzas. The source allows it between stanzas or between lines and supplies no single required metre.
The four- to eight-line stanza repeats several times before a closing tag. The tag sits outside the stanza repeat.
The row’s AAAB leader’s verse and framing chorus illustrate one performance pattern; archived spirituals also include solo and arranged choral performance.
A fixed group response follows an improvised leader’s line. The repeated cycle accelerates; acceleration is an attribute, not an extra passage.
The catalog repeats a four- to eight-line stanza. Dance is optional, and no musical position follows from its presence.
The base unit is one short rhymed stanza of thanks. It may be sung as a round, an optional performance treatment.
The repeated chant and the cantor’s verses sound together; neither follows the other as a new section.
Two published settings of the same psalm use different stanza metres. One alternates eight and six syllables; the other uses eight syllables throughout.
The leader presents one line and the congregation sings that line back slowly. It is line-by-line participation rather than a separate verse and chorus.
Two halves of each prose verse use a recurring chant formula. The illustrated setting closes with a doxology.
The example distinguishes its surrounding antiphon from alternating choral verses and the closing doxology.
The congregation takes up a response and returns to it between verses. The liturgy also permits singing the psalm straight through.
The opening respond, verse and partial return form R–V–R′ in the entry. The second half belongs to the initial respond before it is reused.
The fixed reply follows each separate petition. This models the recurring verbal unit rather than setting a number of petitions.
An officiant’s versicle and the congregation’s answer form a recurring liturgical exchange. The wording can change from pair to pair.
The liturgical text may be chanted or continuously set. Some offices append a doxology to particular canticles; others stand on their own.
A short text of praise may stand alone or close a hymn. The catalog’s named examples differ in lineation, so four lines are illustrative.
Through-composed setting and full choir describe the catalog’s example. Amen is a textual ending in that example, not a definition of choir scoring.
Solo and full-choir passages alternate. “Verse” here marks solo scoring; the row does not identify a pop verse.
The first part of the hymn is sung together; staggered vocal entrances belong to the repeated second half.
The scripture setting employs chordal and fuging writing. The row supplies neither an obligatory order nor the number of these passages.
The catalog’s listed sequence is an example of setting ordinary texts. English Communion orders allow variation, including optional parts and liturgical differences.
The example sets two canticles, each followed by a doxology. Canticle selections vary with the office.
Eight opening lines and a six-line response; line 9 is the conventional turn. CDECDE and CDCDCD are common sestet patterns. The diagram shows the CDECDE option.

The row specifies an alternating octave and two sestet options. These model the catalog entry; the historical Sicilian school does not reduce to a single specimen. The diagram illustrates one of the two sestet choices.
The sentence may cross the boundary between octave and sestet, delaying or softening the expected turn.
The three alternating-rhyme quatrains are followed by a rhyming pair. Those divisions need not be printed as four stanzas.
The last rhyme sound of each of the first two quatrains starts the next. A new EE pair closes.
Four three-line units interlock by their middle rhyme, and the final couplet resolves the chain. Four tercets belong to this sonnet version, not to all terza rima.
Six lines answer to the Italian octave and four and a half to its sestet. An abbreviated final line occupies the eleventh printed position.
A complete sonnet precedes one or more tails. In the catalog version each tail starts with a shortened line followed by two full lines.
Four enclosed-rhyme units span sixteen lines. They can be printed continuously.
Fourteen iambic tetrameter lines form aBaB ccDD eFFe GG. In this notation a, c and e have a trailing unstressed syllable. B, D, F and G end in stress. The catalog reverses the stress legend.
Three quatrains and two closing lines on separate a and b rhymes. The catalog specifies the c-ending version. Individual a/b positions in the quatrains are unspecified.
One word from the borrowed opening recurs in the thirteen succeeding lines. The final two lines also rhyme.
Fourteen lines and a turn are useful reference points, but contemporary practice allows both shape and rhyme to vary; no single tree fits every example.
Seven couplets form fourteen lines of nine to eleven syllables. The second line of each of the first six pairs echoes at the next opening, and the last line echoes the first.
The catalog’s two refrain lines are ambiguous. In the cited specimen the first and last lines of quatrain one make the closing pair; the latter alone ends every preceding quatrain.
Each last line opens the next sonnet, and the final line returns to the first. The number of sonnets can vary.
The first fourteen form a closed crown. Their opening lines in sequence form the fifteenth, or master, sonnet.
A shared subject or progression links a sequence. Numbering is optional; some sequences also link their boundary lines, contrary to the catalog’s blanket exclusion.
In the fixed 19-line form the two opening refrains alternate across four tercets. They meet inside the closing quatrain, rather than forming an extra two-line stanza.

In the 19-line pattern each middle line becomes the final line of the next tercet. The opening pair of refrains returns in the closing quatrain; it does not alternate through the body as in a villanelle.
Labels 1–6 stand for end-words, not rhymes. Each stanza takes the prior positions in the order 6,1,5,2,4,3; the three-line envoi uses all six words.
Two attested constructions differ in both stanza size and envoi. Twelve stanzas of twelve end in six lines; twelve stanzas of six end in three.
Three end-words rotate through three tercets in the orders ABC, CAB and BCA. A single final line gathers all three.
Fifteen positions group 5 + 4 + 6. R is a returning phrase from the opening, not a third rhyme class.
The catalog gives 7 + 6 positions and the independent account gives 7 + 5. The latter arrangement also occurs under the name rondine.
Two readings share a septet, a quintain and a returning short phrase. The catalog starts abaabbR and an independently published specification starts abbaabR.
The lines of stanza one successively close stanzas two through five. The final four full lines take an additional short refrain from the opening phrase.
The first two lines return mid-poem. Closings can repeat only the first or both openings; the catalog’s 13–14 range is incompatible with requiring only line one in every ending.
Two four-position stanzas frame a tercet. The returning short phrase comes from the opening line.
The same four-syllable line occupies positions 1, 3 and 7; lowercase a and b identify rhyme sounds, not repeated lines.
The entry describes a general refrain song with no fixed length. The refrain may be one line or two, and no rhyme inside the two-line alternative is specified.
Two whole lines reappear on top of two rhyme sounds. Lines 1,4,7 match and lines 2,8 match.
Three 8-line stanzas and one 4-line envoi share their final refrain. In the standard form the envoi uses a subset of the stanza rhyme sounds; it does not have to use all three.
Three stanzas share ababbccdcD. The catalog closes with five lines for 35 total. A documented six-line envoi gives 36. Capital D marks the recurring line.
Six stanzas give 48 or 60 lines. An optional envoi yields 52 or 65 in the two documented constructions.
In the historical model, the additional refrain closes the fourth line of each main stanza and the second line of the envoi; the other refrain closes both stanza types.

Five matched eleven-line stanzas plus a five-line envoi give 60 lines. All use the same five-rhyme inventory; the refrain closes each stanza. The five-rhyme inventory applies throughout each stanza and is not a span before a refrain.

The catalog gives the linked-rhyme literary pattern called virelai ancien. A medieval musical virelai instead combines an opening refrain with contrasting music and a return. The two layers are not interchangeable.
The historical literary description alternates the two opening lines as stanza endings, then closes with both in reverse order. The stanza lengths vary.
The catalog describes a nine-line verse pattern made from three aab units, each of 5, 5 and 2 syllables. This cannot be generalized to all medieval narrative or musical lais.
Catalog quatrains have eight syllables per line and a shared refrain in the final position. The sonnet adaptation adds a closing pair.
The first line is repeated at successive local positions 1, 2, 3 and 4 in four quatrains. The row prescribes no rhyme scheme.

The catalog’s general outline allows five to seven matching stanzas and a short envoi. Two more specific constructions rotate end-words through five twelve-line stanzas, with either five or six concluding lines.
The source describes an opening ripresa, then two matching parts and a turn back to the recurring refrain. It gives no fixed number of subsequent stanzas.
One three-line pattern opens with a short line followed by two longer lines. There are also three-long-line and two-line variants, with regional differences in rhyme and assonance.
In a strict construction, the four lines of a borrowed epigraph close successive ten-line stanzas. Other traditions retain the line-by-line return while varying the stanza sizes.
Three long-and-short echo pairs precede a four-line stanza. Its last line gathers the three short replies in order; equal metre across a pair is not required.
The repeating transfer is 2→1 and 4→3 between quatrains. Returning to the opening line is frequent; modern examples vary the rhyme and need not have a circular ending.
The common four-line Malay pattern pairs an opening image with the ensuing meaning across ABAB. UNESCO describes four lines as the commonest length, not the only length.

In the English refrain-bearing pattern, the opening lines and every later second line share rhyme and radif. Five to fifteen is typical, and a poet’s signature is customary rather than mandatory. Signature is a property of the closing couplet, with no assigned first-line position.
Nostalgic prelude, journey and final theme supply one conventional order. A bayt consists of two hemistichs within one verse. English layouts can vary.

Japanese 5–7–5 counts sound units, not English syllables. The Haiku Society of America emphasizes the cut and relationship of images and does not impose three lines or a mandatory English season word. A traditional Japanese template uses 5, 7 and 5 on.
English senryu often use one to three lines. A human observation is central; humor, a cut, and an English 5–7–5 syllable count are not obligatory.

Five short lines are common in English, but Japanese 5–7–5–7–7 counts sound units. The English central turn is a frequent expressive move rather than an exact syllabic boundary. The traditional phrase groups have 5, 7, 5, 7 and 7 sound units.
Comic tanka uses the traditional 5–7–5–7–7 Japanese sound-unit pattern. English syllable counting is an adaptation.
The source gives 5–7–7 and describes the question as frequent. An answer belongs to a possible larger exchange.
The two 5–7–7 units give six phrases. Question and answer are frequent roles rather than obligatory speech acts.
The catalog identifies two voices' tanka. Each has upper and lower phrases; the second replies to the first.
Alternating five- and seven-unit phrases lead into a 5–7–7 close. The catalog also allows a following tanka envoi.
The customary line groups count 7–7–7–5 Japanese sound units, 26 altogether. A refrain can accompany the verse in singing. English syllable counts are adaptations.
Five line breaks normally follow phrases or breaths. Rare four- and six-line versions are documented. No fixed syllable count governs a line.

Linked verse includes several layouts. Renku uses links and shifts; the 36-verse kasen shown here is one layout. Its two folios have four sides of 6, 12, 12 and 6 verses. Its opening, development and close span 6, 24 and 6.
The two-voice version totals 16 lines and the three-voice version 15. The source inventory gives 16 for both. A–C identify voices; all six verses develop one theme.
One or more haiku link with prose. A haiku may close the piece or appear within it.
One or more tanka occur within or after prose. A contest may limit the count for its own entries.
The standard three-line form has two phrases per line and two segments per phrase. The 14–16 syllables per line are approximate; English typography may split these lines.
The catalog describes the traditional four seven-syllable lines on a single rhyme. The four marks apply to line endings.
In the standard chain the sixth positions rhyme; the eight-syllable line's ending supplies the rhyme carried into the next pair.
Each line has four syllables. Across the three lines the linked rhyme moves from syllable four to three to two.
A six-line story unfolds in stanzas of one, two and three lines. Their narrative roles are open.
Three variants illustrate a larger family. Milwr and penfyr have three lines; unodl union has four, with a short toddaid followed by a cywydd couplet.
The unit has two rhyming seven-syllable lines with contrasting final accent. Neither order of stressed and unstressed endings is prescribed.
The catalog prints six segments. The Welsh glossary groups them into two eight-syllable lines and one 16-syllable tail. The diagram shows the divisions within that tail.

Short and long versions open with two or four nine-syllable lines carrying the main rhyme. Their 10+9 closing couplet preserves that rhyme at the first-line break and final line end, with a second rhyme linking the tail to the interior of the final line.

The common pattern has four ten-syllable opening lines and a 10+10 closing couplet. Its shared main rhyme and internal linking rhyme cross the couplet. Other opening lengths are documented. The inventory instead groups the first five lines together.
